title: Iterative shared DIV and REM unit
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz and its 156-cell worst path runs through
forwarding and the execute ALU. The ALU currently infers combinational
32-bit signed and unsigned division and remainder, putting a full divider
on the one-cycle execute path even though DIV/REM are relatively infrequent
in CoreMark. The same logic also contributes substantially to the 12,312
LUT count.

hypothesis.motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz and its 156-cell worst path runs through
forwarding and the execute ALU. The ALU currently infers combinational

on the one-cycle execute path even though DIV/REM are relatively infrequent
in CoreMark. The same logic also contributes substantially to the 12,312
LUT count.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the real-hardware DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU expressions with one
shared, 32-step unsigned restoring divider in the ALU, with start/busy/done
control driven by EX. Latch forwarded operands at start, take magnitudes
for signed operations, and correct quotient or remainder signs at
completion. Handle divide by zero and INT_MIN / -1 exactly as RV32M
specifies. Hold PC and ID/EX from issue through completion, let older
instructions drain, inject invalid EX/MEM bubbles while busy, and capture
the divide result in EX/MEM exactly once on done. A pending dmem stall
takes priority over starting the divider. Keep RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS as an
immediate combinational result without invoking the iterative path, so
the existing formal gate remains tractable. Removing the combinational
divider should raise Fmax enough to outweigh occasional divide latency.

Connect divide busy and completion control to the pipeline so older instructions drain and the divide retires once without losing fetch, redirects, or memory stalls.
Extend stall and bubble arbitration for a multicycle execute operation, preserving dmem-stall and redirect priority.
Adapt DIV/REM vectors to clock the ALU start/busy/done protocol and check the completed exact result, including divide by zero, overflow, signed remainder, and back-to-back operations.
Add a back-to-back DIV/REM and dependent-instruction test with memory backpressure to catch duplicate retirement or lost operands.

title: Move division off the execute critical path
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz and uses 12,312 LUT4s. Its 199.837 ns
worst path runs from forwarding through execute and the combinational ALU.
The four 32-bit divide and remainder operators in that path can create a
deep, replicated quotient network even though division is infrequent in
the CoreMark hot loop. Shortening this path should improve Fmax enough to
outweigh the extra cycles spent on occasional divide instructions.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the execute stage's combinational DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU datapaths
with one shared, iterative 32-bit divider. Latch operands and operation on
issue, compute quotient and remainder together using a radix-2 recurrence,
and release one result into EX/MEM when complete. Launch only when the MEM
stage is free, stall fetch/decode while the divider owns EX, and insert
bubbles downstream so the instruction retires exactly once. Capture the
forwarded operands at launch; preserve redirect and memory-handshake
priority through the interlock. Handle divide by zero and signed overflow
exactly as RV32M specifies. Keep the combinational ALU divider available
for its standalone unit test, but parameterize the ALU so the core instance
omits that logic from synthesis. Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, bypass the
iterative unit and execute the existing one-cycle substitute expressions
so the formal depth and arithmetic contract stay intact. This changes the
execution topology without changing the ISA, RVFI interface, or retirement
order.

title: Fetch-stage two-bit branch direction prediction
motivation:
The current pipeline fetches PC+4 until EX resolves every branch, then
flushes the younger instruction on a taken path. CoreMark repeats many
short loops and data-dependent branches, so this redirect penalty costs
cycles even when the same branch behaved the same way on prior visits.
The measured 200 ns critical path runs through the arithmetic ALU, leaving
room for a small predictor without making fetch the Fmax bottleneck.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 32-entry, PC-indexed table of two-bit saturating direction counters.
On a valid fetch of a legal conditional branch, use the counter to choose
between PC+4 and the B-immediate target; for an unseen entry, predict a
backward branch taken and a forward branch not taken. Predict direct JAL
to its J-immediate target; keep JALR sequential until EX resolves it.
Carry the predicted next PC with the instruction into EX. EX compares it
with the resolved next PC, including misalignment-trap behavior, and
redirects and flushes only on a mismatch. Train a conditional-branch
counter once when its EX instruction advances, never on a held bus cycle
or a wrong-path bubble. This should remove most recurring taken-branch
bubbles with modest state and little effect on the dominant ALU timing path.

title: Narrow ID/EX flush to control and validity
motivation:
After the iterative divider improvement, the 48.181 MHz champion is
limited by a 26.444 ns path from the register file through execute,
fetch, and hazard logic into an ID/EX operand register. Redirect and
load-use flushes currently zero the entire wide ID/EX payload, so the
late flush decision controls every operand and metadata flop. This
timing path limits fitness even though a flushed instruction only
needs its side effects and retirement suppressed.

hypothesis.motivation:
After the iterative divider improvement, the 48.181 MHz champion is
limited by a 26.444 ns path from the register file through execute,
fetch, and hazard logic into an ID/EX operand register. Redirect and

late flush decision controls every operand and metadata flop. This

needs its side effects and retirement suppressed.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Change the ID/EX register so reset still clears the full payload, but
redirect and load-use flushes clear only ctrl and valid. Give the data
fields an enable controlled solely by the existing stall signal: on a
redirect without a stall they may capture the wrong-path payload, while
on a load-use flush with a stall they hold their prior values. Either
payload is harmless because ctrl is zero and valid is false. Preserve
flush-over-stall priority for ctrl and valid. This removes the late
EX-to-ID flush selection from the 32-bit operand and metadata register
inputs, cutting fanout and logic depth on the measured critical path
without adding pipeline stages or changing instruction throughput.
Check that a flushed branch, store, register write, or divide cannot
produce a side effect and that stall plus flush arbitration is correct.

changes.description: Split ID/EX register updates: reset clears all fields; data fields use only the stall enable, while flush clears ctrl and valid with priority over stall.
Cover taken-branch and load-use flushes, including overlapping memory stalls, to confirm wrong-path control never retires or writes state.

title: Use control-only bubbles to cut branch feedback
motivation:
After the iterative divider raised Fmax to 48.181 MHz, the measured worst
path runs from a register-file bit through execute, fetch, hazard control,
and back into an ID/EX operand register. A resolved branch or jump currently
substitutes a NOP into the entire combinational fetch instruction bus and
clears every ID/EX data register. That makes branch resolution feed decode,
register-file read, and the operand-register input muxes before the ID/EX
clock edge. The 38-cell, 26.444 ns path now limits fitness.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the current pipeline depth and branch resolution point, but represent
a killed younger instruction as a control-only bubble. On redirect, drive
IF/ID's instruction directly from imem instead of muxing in a NOP; retain
the imem-not-ready bubble behavior. At the ID/EX clock edge, clear valid
and the complete decoded control word, but leave operand and metadata
registers untouched because zero control makes their contents inert.
Ensure redirect wins over a simultaneous wrong-path load-use comparison;
preserve dmem hold/replay and PC redirect priority. This removes the
execute-to-fetch-to-decode operand loop and the redirect-to-operand-register
flush path while preserving retirement order and branch penalty. Reducing
those two fanout paths should raise Fmax without changing CoreMark cycles.

title: Tagged branch target prediction on the shared-divider core
motivation:
The shared iterative divider raised Fmax to 48.181 MHz, making lost branch
cycles a material part of fitness. A previous fetch direction predictor
reduced CoreMark cycles by 6.5%, but it was evaluated on a core still
limited to about 5.5 MHz by combinational division. The present core still
waits until EX to redirect every taken branch, JAL, and JALR, discarding
younger work each time.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 32-entry direct-mapped, PC-tagged branch target buffer in fetch.
Each entry holds a resolved target and a two-bit saturating direction
counter. On a tag hit with the counter in a taken state, fetch uses the
saved target without decoding the fetched instruction; otherwise it uses
PC+4. EX compares
the instruction's recorded predicted next PC against its resolved next PC
and redirects only on a mismatch. Train the buffer once when a valid legal
control-flow instruction advances from EX, including JALR, and suppress
training and correction while EX is held by an older dmem stall or division.
Allocate entries on taken branches and jumps only, initialize new branch
counters as weakly taken, update existing branch counters on both outcomes,
and keep jumps strongly taken. A full PC tag prevents unrelated instructions
from using stale targets. Storing the target avoids a B/J immediate adder on the fetch
feedback path and should recover recurring taken branches and stable JALR
targets with less Fmax cost than calculating targets in fetch.

title: Isolate memory address and bubble payload critical paths
motivation:
The current 124.85-fitness core has two nearly equal worst paths at about
24.84 ns. The first runs from a register-file output through a DSP
multiplier and the general ALU result selector to a data-memory address
pin, although loads and stores need only base plus immediate. The second
runs through EX branch comparison, fetch correction, and the reset of an
ID/EX operand register. Neither the multiplier result nor the operand
payload of a killed instruction needs to participate in these paths.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Isolate the two timed side-effect paths from unused data. Give EX a
dedicated forwarded-rs1-plus-immediate address register in EX/MEM and
drive the MEM-stage address, byte-lane selection, and misalignment checks
from it; keep the original ALU result register for writeback and forwarding.
This prevents DSP multiplication and its result selector from feeding the
data-memory address pins. On ID/EX redirect or load-use bubbles, clear
valid and decoded control while allowing operand and metadata fields to
hold or capture harmless values, so the late branch decision no longer
resets every operand bit. Preserve reset, stall priority, forwarding,
divider behavior, precise retirement, and all memory and trap semantics.
With both measured paths shortened, Fmax should improve without changing
CoreMark instruction count or normal pipeline latency.

title: Isolate decode and memory address timing from the general ALU
motivation:
The 52.327 MHz champion has two nearly equal worst paths. One runs from
the block-RAM register file through forwarding and a multiplier DSP to
the data-memory address input (24.845 ns); the other runs from the same
register file through branch correction into decode (24.843 ns). Clearing
only one path leaves the other limiting Fmax. A local prototype of the
combined structural change scored 134.27 versus 124.85, with unchanged
CoreMark cycles (4,191,341) and correct benchmark CRCs.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the 32x32 integer register file explicitly flop-backed so Gowin
keeps the intended ID/EX register boundary instead of folding the read

decoded immediate on a separate address-generation lane and register it
as EX/MEM.mem_addr. Drive the data-memory address, byte selection,
alignment check, and RVFI memory address from this registered field.
Leave the general ALU result on the arithmetic and writeback lane, so
multiplier outputs cannot feed the data-memory address path. Preserve
the existing forwarding priorities, divider interlock, predictor,
memory backpressure, traps, and single retirement. This restores the
decode/execute timing boundary and removes the multiplier from the
memory address cone without adding instruction latency.

title: Predict direct targets from fetch instruction and reserve BTB for JALR
motivation:
The current direct-mapped BTB stores a full target for every taken branch,
JAL, and JALR, although branch and JAL targets are already encoded in the
fetched instruction. A CoreMark control-flow trace between the timing
markers has about 593,000 control transfers; a retire-order model of the
32-entry BTB estimates about 57,000 prediction misses, including about
20,600 tag misses. Direct transfers evict each other and indirect targets
from this small table. Separating their prediction paths can reduce both
conflicts and target-storage cost.

hypothesis.motivation:

hypothesis.hypothesis:
In IF, recognize legal conditional branches and JALs from io_imemData
when the fetch is valid. Form their B/J PC-relative targets in parallel
with a 256-entry, two-bit direction table indexed by an XOR fold of PC
bits [9:2] and [17:10]. Predict JAL taken unconditionally and a branch
taken when its direction counter is taken; otherwise use PC+4. Use a
backward-taken, forward-not-taken default for an uninitialized counter.
Keep a small eight-entry tagged target table only for legal JALR, which
has no instruction-encoded absolute target. EX continues to compare each
instruction's recorded predicted next PC with its resolved next PC and
correct any miss; train the direction or indirect-target table exactly
once when a valid, legal control transfer advances from EX. Gate direct
target use on 4-byte alignment, preserve redirect priority over imem
stalls, and never train on held, trapped, or wrong-path instructions.
The compact direction and indirect-target state should reduce BTB
interference and may offset the timing cost of the fetch target adder.
A simplified retire-order trace model estimates roughly 43,000 misses
for this split predictor, versus 57,000 for the current BTB.

title: Predecode operand forwarding before execute
motivation:
The current 56.278 MHz design spends its 23.083 ns worst path from an
ID/EX source-register number through the forwarding comparisons and
execute ALU to the EX/MEM result register. The register numbers of both
possible producers are already known one cycle earlier, while the
consumer is being decoded. Removing the comparisons from the execute
path should raise Fmax without changing CoreMark cycles or adding state
to the data path.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current 56.278 MHz design spends its 23.083 ns worst path from an
ID/EX source-register number through the forwarding comparisons and
execute ALU to the EX/MEM result register. The register numbers of both

consumer is being decoded. Removing the comparisons from the execute
path should raise Fmax without changing CoreMark cycles or adding state

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Compute the two forwarding choices in ID when an instruction is accepted:
compare each fetched source register against the current ID/EX destination
for next cycle's EX/MEM bypass, then against the current EX/MEM destination
for next cycle's MEM/WB bypass. Give the younger producer priority and
suppress x0 matches. Register the choices alongside the decoded operands,
and drive EX's existing three-way operand muxes directly from those bits.
Preserve the existing load-use bubble, write-first register-file bypass,
divide hold, redirect flush, and memory-stall priority. During a dmem stall,
hold the saved choices with ID/EX; the existing MEM/WB data retention keeps
the selected older value available when EX resumes. This should remove two
five-bit comparators and priority logic from the forwarding-to-ALU timing
cone, with no extra cycle on the normal path.

title: Stage multiplication operands outside the forwarding path
motivation:
The 134.27-fitness champion is limited by a 23.083 ns path from an
ID/EX source register through forwarding and the multiply-capable ALU
into EX/MEM. Its dedicated memory address lane has already removed the
data-memory pin from this path. A structural timing boundary before the
multiplier can shorten the worst path without slowing ordinary integer,
branch, load, or store instructions.

multiplier cascade into separate clock-to-clock paths; the expected

Preserve same-cycle bypass priority, memory backpressure, branch

title: Compact 64-entry branch target buffer with short tags
motivation:
The current 32-entry direct-mapped BTB is useful, but the prior control-flow
trace attributed roughly 20,600 misses to tag conflicts. A larger table
should recover some of those cycles. The previous 256-entry split predictor
lost Fmax because its direction and JALR structures added substantial LUT
area, so the existing single-table organization is the better starting point.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Expand the unified BTB from 32 to 64 entries while narrowing each stored
tag to 12 PC bits above the six-bit word index. Keep full 32-bit targets and
two-bit saturating counters, including strongly-taken JAL/JALR training.
The 64-entry short-tag table should reduce direct-mapped conflicts with a
modest storage increase, and its narrower equality check should keep the
fetch-to-PC path short. The stored bits distinguish all aligned instruction
addresses in the permitted 1 MiB program region. If an alias ever occurs,
EX still compares the recorded predicted next PC with the resolved next PC
and redirects on any mismatch.
Preserve training only when a valid legal control transfer advances from EX,
plus existing redirect priority and bus-stall behavior. Test partial-tag
collision and stale-target recovery so wrong-path work cannot retire.

title: Register branch predictor training before BTB update
motivation:
The 66.728 MHz champion's worst measured path has 38 logic cells from the
MEM/WB writeback selection through execute branch resolution to a BTB
counter register. Branch prediction is useful, but its training update
need not occur on the same edge as branch resolution. Breaking this
feedback path should improve Fmax without adding a cycle to instruction
execution or changing the memory interface.

hypothesis.motivation:

MEM/WB writeback selection through execute branch resolution to a BTB
counter register. Branch prediction is useful, but its training update
need not occur on the same edge as branch resolution. Breaking this

execution or changing the memory interface.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Put a one-entry training register at the input of the existing BTB update
logic. On each clock edge, capture the EX stage's qualified train_valid,
train_pc, train_target, train_taken, and train_jump signals; on the next
edge, apply that registered event to the existing tag, target, and
saturating-counter update. Capture a new event on every edge so consecutive
branches are trained in order without drops. Reset the pending valid bit,
and preserve the existing EX qualification that excludes held, invalid,
illegal, and misaligned instructions. Keep EX redirect and resolved next PC
immediate; only predictor state learns one cycle later. This retimes the
writeback-to-BTB feedback path into two shorter clock-to-clock paths.
An immediately repeated branch can see the previous counter state for one
extra fetch, but any resulting misprediction is corrected by the unchanged
EX redirect path and should have negligible CoreMark cycle cost.

title: Register branch predictor training before BTB updates
motivation:
The 159.20-fitness champion is limited by a 20.354 ns, 38-cell path from
the MEM/WB load-result select through execute to a fetch-stage BTB counter
write. Forwarded branch operands determine the outcome, and the same cycle
also performs tag lookup, saturating-counter logic, and indexed BTB writes.
The prior staged multiplier lost CoreMark cycles and still ended at the BTB;
isolating predictor maintenance directly targets the measured endpoint.

title: Pipeline BTB training behind branch resolution
motivation:
The 159.20-fitness champion's measured worst path starts at MEM/WB,
crosses forwarded EX branch resolution, and ends at a BTB counter write.
A larger predictor already lost more Fmax than its modest cycle savings
could recover. The existing 32-entry BTB therefore needs a shorter
training path rather than more entries.

current replacement and saturation rules. This moves tag lookup, hit
